items.value: Motupalli was the great seaport of the Kakatiya kingdom
items.reasoning: Motupalli, on the Andhra coast, was the principal port of the Kakatiyas of Warangal. Ganapatideva issued the celebrated Motupalli Abhaya Shasanam, a charter guaranteeing the safety of foreign merchants and their goods, and Marco Polo describes the port's trade in his account of the region. Machilipatnam (Masulipatnam) rose to prominence later, under the Qutb Shahis and the European companies; Kakinada is a modern port; and Nelluru (Nellore) was an inland administrative and temple town, not a Kakatiya seaport.

items.value: Statements 1 and 2 are correct — the GCCA is an EU initiative giving technical and financial support to targeted developing countries; statement 3 is false, WRI and WBCSD coordinate the Greenhouse Gas Protocol, not the GCCA
items.reasoning: The Global Climate Change Alliance was launched in 2007 by the European Commission, so statement 1 is correct. Its stated purpose is to help the poorest and most vulnerable developing countries — chiefly Least Developed Countries and Small Island Developing States — integrate climate change into their development policies and national budgets, through technical assistance and grant finance, so statement 2 is correct. Statement 3 attaches the wrong body: the World Resources Institute and the World Business Council for Sustainable Development jointly run the Greenhouse Gas Protocol, a corporate emissions-accounting standard, and have no coordinating role in the GCCA.

items.value: Only statement 2 is correct — Sautrantika and Sammitiya were Buddhist, not Jain, sects; the Sarvastivadins did hold that phenomena's constituents exist perpetually in latent form
items.reasoning: Sautrantika and Sammitiya (Sammatiya) both belong to the eighteen early schools of BUDDHISM — the Sautrantikas took the sutras rather than the Abhidharma as authoritative, and the Sammitiyas were a branch of the Pudgalavada tradition — so statement 1 is wrong in assigning them to Jainism. Statement 2 correctly states the defining doctrine of the Sarvastivada, whose very name means 'the theory that all exists': the dharmas constituting phenomena are held to exist in past, present and future, persisting in a latent condition rather than being wholly momentary. That doctrine is precisely what distinguished the Sarvastivadins from the strict momentariness of other schools.

items.value: Only Lebanon and Syria have a Mediterranean coastline; Jordan and Iraq do not
items.reasoning: Lebanon's entire western frontier is the Mediterranean, and Syria has a Mediterranean coast running from the Turkish border down to Lebanon, including the ports of Latakia and Tartus. Jordan is effectively landlocked apart from a very short frontage on the Gulf of Aqaba at the head of the Red Sea, and Iraq's only sea access is a narrow outlet on the Persian Gulf near Umm Qasr. Neither touches the Mediterranean, so only the pair 3 and 4 qualifies.

items.value: Both statements are wrong — NIIF is not an organ of NITI Aayog (it is a fund set up by the Ministry of Finance and registered with SEBI as an AIF), and its corpus is of the order of Rs 40,000 crore, not Rs 4,00,000 crore
items.reasoning: The National Investment and Infrastructure Fund was created by the Government of India through the Ministry of Finance as an investment vehicle, registered with SEBI as a Category II Alternative Investment Fund and run by a professional fund-management company; NITI Aayog is a policy think-tank and has no ownership of it, so statement 1 is wrong. Statement 2 overstates the corpus by an order of magnitude: NIIF was announced with a planned corpus of about Rs 40,000 crore, of which the Government's share is roughly 49 per cent (about Rs 20,000 crore), the balance to be raised from domestic and foreign investors.

items.value: The Global Infrastructure Facility is a World Bank Group platform that helps prepare and structure complex infrastructure PPPs so as to mobilise private and institutional capital
items.reasoning: The Global Infrastructure Facility was launched by the World Bank Group as a global collaboration platform. It works upstream — helping governments prepare, structure and bring to market complex infrastructure public-private partnerships in emerging markets so that private sector and institutional investor money (pension funds, insurers, sovereign funds) can be crowded in. It is neither an ASEAN body financed by the Asian Development Bank (A), nor an OECD-anchored bankers' club (C), nor a UNCTAD-funded programme (D); UNCTAD is a trade and development research and policy body and does not finance infrastructure.

items.value: A nomination can be filed by any citizen of India who is registered as an elector in a constituency — residence in the particular constituency being contested is not required
items.reasoning: Section 4 of the Representation of the People Act, 1951 requires that a person be an elector for a parliamentary constituency in India in order to be chosen to fill a Lok Sabha seat. So the qualifying condition is enrolment in an electoral roll, not residence in the seat being fought — which is why candidates routinely contest from constituencies they do not live in, making B wrong. A is wrong because mere residence in India is not enough (a non-citizen resident cannot stand), and D is wrong because citizenship alone does not suffice — an unregistered citizen, or one disqualified from the roll, cannot file.

items.value: Only statement 3 is correct — Pulicat Lake lies in two States (Andhra Pradesh and Tamil Nadu); the Himalayas and the Western Ghats each extend over more than five States
items.reasoning: The Indian Himalaya runs through far more than five States — Jammu and Kashmir, Himachal Pradesh, Uttarakhand, Sikkim, West Bengal and Arunachal Pradesh at the least, with the eastern ranges continuing into Assam, Nagaland, Manipur and Mizoram — so the word 'only' in statement 1 defeats it. The Western Ghats, as delimited by the Government of India for Ecologically Sensitive Area purposes and by the Gadgil and Kasturirangan panels, run through six States: Gujarat, Maharashtra, Goa, Karnataka, Kerala and Tamil Nadu, so 'five only' is also wrong. Pulicat, the second-largest brackish lagoon in India, straddles the Andhra Pradesh-Tamil Nadu boundary and lies in exactly those two States, so statement 3 stands. RUNNER-UP: C (2 and 3 only) — it wins if the Western Ghats are counted as spanning only Maharashtra, Goa, Karnataka, Kerala and Tamil Nadu, the older five-State description that omits the northern Gujarat (Dangs) extension. The whole item pivots on whether Gujarat is counted, and a reviewer should look there first.

items.value: BOD measures organic pollution load in water — a pollution assay for aquatic ecosystems
items.reasoning: Biological (Biochemical) Oxygen Demand is the quantity of dissolved oxygen consumed by aerobic micro-organisms while decomposing the organic matter in a water sample, conventionally measured over five days at 20 degrees Celsius. A high BOD means a heavy load of biodegradable organic matter — sewage, food-processing effluent, agricultural runoff — which strips oxygen from the water and asphyxiates fish and other aquatic life. It is therefore a standard index of organic water pollution, and has nothing to do with oxygen in blood, in forests, or at high altitude.

items.value: Statements 1 and 3 are correct; statement 2 is false because UN-Habitat's partners are not restricted to governments and local authorities
items.reasoning: UN-Habitat is the UN programme mandated by the General Assembly to promote socially and environmentally sustainable towns and cities with the goal of adequate shelter for all, which is statement 1 almost verbatim. Statement 3 is likewise correct: UN-Habitat's work is tied to the wider UN objective of reducing poverty and improving access to safe drinking water and basic sanitation, and it runs a Water and Sanitation Trust Fund to that end. Statement 2 fails on the word 'only' — UN-Habitat works with a wide partner base that includes non-governmental organisations, community and grassroots groups, professional and research institutions, the private sector and other UN agencies, not just governments and municipal authorities.

items.value: Only statement 2 is correct — NSQF explicitly recognises informal and non-formal learning through Recognition of Prior Learning, but it does aim at mobility between vocational and general education
items.reasoning: The National Skills Qualification Framework organises qualifications into levels defined by learning outcomes rather than by how the learning was acquired, and it provides for Recognition of Prior Learning so that competence gained informally on the job can be assessed and certified. Statement 1's 'only through formal learning' therefore inverts one of the framework's central features. Statement 2 is a stated objective of the NSQF: by making qualifications comparable and outcome-based it enables horizontal and vertical movement between the vocational stream and general education, so that a vocational qualification is no longer a dead end.

items.value: Dyarchy meant splitting the provincial subjects into two categories — 'transferred' subjects administered by ministers responsible to the legislature, and 'reserved' subjects retained by the Governor and his executive council
items.reasoning: Dyarchy was introduced in the provinces by the Government of India Act, 1919 (the Montagu-Chelmsford reforms). Subjects were first divided between the Centre and the provinces, and then the provincial list was itself split in two: transferred subjects such as education, local self-government, public health and agriculture were placed under Indian ministers answerable to the legislative council, while reserved subjects such as police, land revenue, justice and irrigation stayed with the Governor acting with his executive council. Option A describes bicameralism, which the 1919 Act also introduced at the Centre but which is a separate feature; B describes federal division of powers; C describes the Home Government-Government of India relationship, not dyarchy.

items.value: Both statements are wrong — the National Career Service is a Ministry of Labour and Employment initiative, not DoPT's, and it serves all jobseekers rather than being aimed at 'uneducated youth'
items.reasoning: The National Career Service was launched in 2015 as a mission-mode project of the Ministry of Labour and Employment, which transformed the old National Employment Service and its employment exchanges into an online portal linking jobseekers, employers, skill providers, counsellors and placement organisations. The Department of Personnel and Training is concerned with civil-service personnel policy and recruitment to government posts, so statement 1 misattributes the scheme. Statement 2 is right that the launch was in mission mode but wrong in its target: the NCS is open to jobseekers across the educational spectrum, including graduates and skilled workers, and is not a scheme confined to uneducated youth.

items.value: S4A is an RBI scheme for reworking the financial structure — splitting sustainable from unsustainable debt — of large corporate borrowers in genuine difficulty
items.reasoning: The Scheme for Sustainable Structuring of Stressed Assets was issued by the Reserve Bank of India in June 2016 to deal with large stressed corporate accounts. Under it, an independent agency determines how much of the borrower's debt can be serviced from existing cash flows; that 'sustainable' portion is retained as debt on existing terms, while the unsustainable remainder is converted into equity or equity-like instruments held by the lenders. It is thus a bank-regulatory restructuring tool, not an environmental costing procedure (A), not a disinvestment plan for public sector undertakings (C), and not a provision of the Insolvency and Bankruptcy Code (D), which is a separate statutory resolution framework administered through the NCLT.

items.value: Only statement 2 is correct — the CCAC is a UNEP-hosted voluntary partnership, not a G20 initiative, but it does target methane, black carbon and HFCs
items.reasoning: The Climate and Clean Air Coalition was launched in 2012 by the United Nations Environment Programme together with six founding countries (Bangladesh, Canada, Ghana, Mexico, Sweden and the United States) and has since grown into a broad voluntary partnership of states, intergovernmental bodies and civil-society organisations; it is not an initiative of the G20, so statement 1 is wrong. Statement 2 is correct: the Coalition's mandate is short-lived climate pollutants, and its priority pollutants are black carbon, methane and hydrofluorocarbons, along with tropospheric ozone, all of which have short atmospheric lifetimes so that cutting them yields quick climate and air-quality benefits.

items.value: Only statement 2 is correct — the IOD is defined by the temperature contrast between the tropical WESTERN and tropical EASTERN INDIAN Ocean, not the eastern Pacific, but it can indeed modulate El Nino's effect on the monsoon
items.reasoning: The Indian Ocean Dipole is measured as the difference in sea surface temperature between the western equatorial Indian Ocean (off East Africa, the Arabian Sea sector) and the south-eastern equatorial Indian Ocean (off Sumatra and Java). Statement 1 replaces the eastern Indian Ocean pole with the tropical eastern Pacific, which is the domain of El Nino and a different phenomenon altogether, so it is wrong as printed. Statement 2 is correct and is why the IOD is watched during monsoon forecasting: a strongly positive IOD warms the western Indian Ocean and enhances moisture convergence over India, and has repeatedly been observed to offset or mask the rainfall deficit that an El Nino year would otherwise produce.

items.value: The Chambal River (National Chambal Sanctuary) is the best place to see gharials in the wild
items.reasoning: The gharial is a fish-eating, narrow-snouted crocodilian of clear, fast-flowing rivers with deep pools and sandbanks for basking and nesting. The National Chambal Sanctuary, on the Chambal across Madhya Pradesh, Rajasthan and Uttar Pradesh, holds by far the largest surviving breeding population and is the mainstay of gharial conservation in India. Bhitarkanika's mangrove creeks are saltwater crocodile habitat, Pulicat is a brackish coastal lagoon known for flamingos and other waterbirds, and Deepor Beel is a freshwater wetland in Assam noted for migratory birds — none of them is gharial country.

items.value: Only statement 2 is correct — IONS is a voluntary maritime-cooperation initiative of Indian Ocean littoral navies, but its inaugural edition was in 2008, not 2015
items.reasoning: The Indian Ocean Naval Symposium was conceived by the Indian Navy and its inaugural gathering was held at New Delhi in February 2008, with India holding the first chairmanship; by 2015 the chair had passed on through the UAE and South Africa to Australia. Statement 1's date is therefore wrong, even though it correctly names India and the Indian Navy for the inaugural edition. Statement 2 accurately describes the forum: it is a voluntary, consultative initiative bringing together the navies of the littoral states of the Indian Ocean Region to increase maritime cooperation, share information and build common understanding on regional maritime security.

items.value: The Bodhisattva Padmapani painting is at Ajanta
items.reasoning: The Padmapani — the bodhisattva holding a blue lotus, painted with downcast eyes and a serene, inward expression — occupies the wall beside the shrine antechamber of Cave 1 at Ajanta, paired with the Bodhisattva Vajrapani, and is the single most reproduced image of Indian mural painting. Ellora and Badami are renowned for rock-cut sculpture and architecture rather than for this mural; Bagh (Madhya Pradesh) does have important Buddhist paintings closely related in style to Ajanta's, but the Padmapani is an Ajanta work.

items.value: Only pair 1 is correct — Chaliha Sahib is a Sindhi festival; Nanda Raj Jaat is an Uttarakhand (Garhwal-Kumaon) pilgrimage, not Gond, and Wari-Warkari is Maharashtrian, not Santhal
items.reasoning: Chaliha Sahib is the forty-day observance kept by the Sindhi community in devotion to Jhulelal, the community's water deity, so pair 1 is correctly matched. The Nanda Devi Raj Jat is a Himalayan pilgrimage held roughly once in twelve years in Uttarakhand, in which the image of the goddess Nanda is carried in procession from Nauti up to Homkund; it belongs to the Garhwali and Kumaoni hill communities, not to the Gonds of central India. The Wari is the annual foot-pilgrimage of the Warkari sect of Maharashtra, who carry the padukas of Dnyaneshwar and Tukaram to Pandharpur on Ashadhi Ekadashi; it has no connection with the Santhals, an Adivasi people of Jharkhand, West Bengal and Odisha.

items.value: All three practices can help conserve water — zero tillage and retained crop residue both cut evaporation and runoff, and gypsum applied before irrigation improves infiltration in sodic, crust-forming soils
items.reasoning: Reduced or zero tillage leaves the soil undisturbed, preserving pore structure and the surface mulch, which lowers evaporative loss and improves the soil's capacity to take in and hold water, so practice 1 helps. Leaving crop residue in the field works the same way from the surface: the residue shades the soil, reduces direct evaporation, slows runoff and improves infiltration, so practice 3 helps. Practice 2 is the judgement call: gypsum is best known as an amendment for sodic and alkali soils, where its calcium displaces exchangeable sodium, flocculates dispersed clay and breaks up the surface crust; applied before irrigation this raises the infiltration rate so that water enters the root zone instead of ponding and running off, which is a genuine gain in irrigation water-use efficiency. Since the stem asks only what 'can help' in water conservation, all three qualify. RUNNER-UP: C (1 and 3 only) — it wins if gypsum is read strictly as a soil-reclamation chemical whose purpose is removing sodium rather than saving water, and indeed the leaching that follows gypsum application on sodic land consumes extra water rather than saving it. The item turns entirely on how permissively 'can help in water conservation' is read for statement 2.

items.value: Only statement 3 is correct — the Soil Health Card aims at balanced, judicious fertilizer use; it has nothing to do with expanding irrigated area or with bank loan assessment
items.reasoning: The Soil Health Card Scheme tests farmers' soil for its macro- and micro-nutrient status, pH, organic carbon and other parameters, and issues a card carrying crop-wise recommendations on the nutrients and fertilizers actually needed. Its purpose is to correct the indiscriminate and unbalanced application of fertilizers — especially excess urea — so statement 3 is correct. Statement 1 belongs to a different scheme: expanding the area under assured irrigation is the objective of the Pradhan Mantri Krishi Sinchayee Yojana. Statement 2 is simply not part of the scheme's design; the card is an agronomic advisory to the farmer, and quantum of crop credit is fixed by the scale of finance for the crop and the land held, not by soil quality.

items.value: All three pairs are correctly matched — lead in lipstick, brominated vegetable oil in soft drinks, and monosodium glutamate in Chinese fast food
items.reasoning: Lead has repeatedly been detected as a contaminant in lipsticks, entering through the mineral pigments used to colour them, and regulators have had to set permissible limits — a well-known consumer-safety controversy. Brominated vegetable oil is a vegetable oil bonded with bromine and used as an emulsifier to keep citrus flavouring evenly dispersed in soft drinks; it is contentious because of bromine accumulation in body tissue and has been restricted or banned in several countries. Monosodium glutamate is the flavour enhancer characteristically associated with Chinese fast food, long debated under the label 'Chinese restaurant syndrome'. All three associations are exactly the unwanted or controversial chemicals the question describes.

items.value: All three are genuine OLED advantages over LCDs — fabrication on flexible plastic substrates, roll-up displays that can be embedded in clothing, and transparent displays
items.reasoning: An OLED is an emissive device: each pixel is a thin organic film that generates its own light, so the display needs no glass backlight assembly, no diffuser and no rigid liquid-crystal cell. The organic layers can be deposited on thin plastic film, which makes flexible substrates possible (statement 1) and in turn makes bendable and roll-up panels light and robust enough to be built into fabric and clothing (statement 2). Because the emissive stack can be made from very thin layers with transparent electrodes, an OLED panel can be substantially see-through when switched off, giving transparent displays (statement 3) — something an LCD cannot readily do since it depends on a backlight and polarisers behind the panel.

items.value: Only Arasavalli is famous for a Sun temple; Amarakantak is a Narmada-source pilgrimage centre and Omkareshwar is a Shiva Jyotirlinga site
items.reasoning: Arasavalli, near Srikakulam in Andhra Pradesh, has the Suryanarayana Swamy temple, one of the very few functioning Sun temples in India and celebrated for the alignment that lets the sun's rays fall on the deity at certain times of the year. Amarakantak in Madhya Pradesh, on the Maikal range, is revered as the source of the Narmada and is associated with Narmada and Shiva shrines, not with surya worship. Omkareshwar, on an island in the Narmada, houses one of the twelve Jyotirlingas and is likewise a Shaiva centre. So only pair 1 answers the stem.
